hook.text: Why do you remember 'Just Do It' but forget thousands of other slogans?

buildup.text: Chip and Dan Heath's 'Made to Stick' identifies six principles: Simple, Unexpected, Concrete, Credible, Emotional,.

discovery.text: Sticky slogans hit at least three: 'Think Different' is simple, unexpected, and emotional. That's why it endures.

twist.text: Clever slogans often fail the stickiness test. Puns are forgettable. Simplicity and emotion outlast wordplay every time.

climax.text: The stickiest slogans become part of the language itself. 'Where's the beef?' entered everyday speech.

punchline.text: Simple, unexpected, emotional. Three traits of slogans that stick.

quiz.question: What are the six principles of 'sticky' ideas?
options: Simple, Unexpected, Concrete, Credible, Emotional, Story
Fast, Loud, Visual, Funny, Short, Clever
Bold, Bright, Big, Brave, Brief, Beautiful

topics.title: Brevity Is the Soul of Slogans

hook.text: 'Got Milk?' Two words. 'Just Do It.' Three words. 'Think Different.' Two words. The greatest slogans are the shortest.

buildup.text: Working memory holds 7 items, plus or minus 2. A slogan with 2-4 words fits easily. Longer slogans strain recall.

discovery.text: Slogans under 5 words are recalled 80% more than those over 10. Each extra word reduces memorability significantly.

twist.text: 'Because You're Worth It' is 4 words and L'Oréal's most valuable asset. Short doesn't mean shallow—it means distilled.

climax.text: The writer's challenge: compress the brand's entire promise into the fewest possible words. Distillation is the skill.

punchline.text: Two words can be worth billions. Brevity is a slogan's power.

quiz.question: How much more are slogans under 5 words recalled compared to longer ones?

hook.text: 'See the USA in your Chevrolet.' It rhymes and it sticks.

buildup.text: The 'rhyme-as-reason' effect: McGlone and Tofighbakhsh proved that rhymes are perceived as more accurate and believable.

discovery.text: 'An apple a day keeps the doctor away' isn't medical advice—it's a rhyme. The form convinces more than the content.

twist.text: Even simple rhythm without rhyme works. 'Ba da ba ba bah, I'm lovin' it.' The beat makes it memorable, not the meaning.

climax.text: Johnny Cochran's 'If it doesn't fit, you must acquit' won an acquittal partly because the jury remembered the rhyme.

punchline.text: Rhymes feel truer. Rhythm sticks in memory. Sound sells.

quiz.question: What is the 'rhyme-as-reason' effect?
options: Rhyming statements are perceived as more truthful

hook.text: 'Because You're Worth It' doesn't mention shampoo. It speaks to self-worth.

buildup.text: L'Oréal's slogan, written by Ilon Specht in 1973, was a feminist statement. It told women they deserved luxury.

discovery.text: Emotional slogans outperform functional ones.

twist.text: The emotion must match the brand. 'Just Do It' is motivational for Nike but would be absurd for a funeral home.

climax.text: The greatest slogans tap into universal emotions: belonging, freedom, worth, adventure. The product is just the vehicle.

punchline.text: Touch an emotion, own a memory. Feelings outlast features.

quiz.question: Who wrote 'Because You're Worth It'?

hook.text: 'Have It Your Way' is a slogan. 'I'm Lovin' It' is a tagline. 'Where's the Beef?' is a catchphrase.

buildup.text: A slogan defines the brand long-term. A tagline accompanies a specific campaign.

discovery.text: Nike's slogan is 'Just Do It'—permanent. 'Find Your Greatness' was a campaign tagline—temporary. Different lifespans.

twist.text: Some taglines become slogans when a campaign is too good to retire. 'A Diamond Is Forever' started as a campaign line.

climax.text: Understanding the difference helps copywriters pitch correctly: slogans need board approval; taglines need creative.

punchline.text: Slogans are permanent. Taglines are seasonal. Know the difference.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a slogan and a tagline?
options: Slogans are long-term brand identity; taglines are campaign-specific

hook.text: In 1988, Nike was losing to Reebok. Three words turned the brand around. 'Just Do It' became the voice of ambition.

buildup.text: Dan Wieden drew partial inspiration from a convicted killer's last words.

discovery.text: Nike's revenue jumped from $877 million to $9.2 billion in 10 years. The slogan didn't sell shoes—it sold a mindset.

twist.text: The slogan works for running, basketball, soccer, and even wheelchair athletes.

climax.text: After 35+ years, 'Just Do It' is still used. It's the most recognized commercial slogan in the English language.

punchline.text: $877M to $9.2B. Three words did what no product could alone.

quiz.question: How much did Nike's revenue grow in the decade after 'Just Do It'?

hook.text: In 1997, Apple was 90 days from bankruptcy. Steve Jobs came back and launched 'Think Different.' It was a resurrection.

buildup.text: The campaign showed Einstein, Lennon, MLK—no products. It told rebels they belonged at Apple. Identity before features.

discovery.text: Apple stock rose 33% within a year of the campaign.

twist.text: Grammatically, it should be 'Think Differently.' The deliberate error made it more memorable and reinforced rebellion.

climax.text: The slogan made Apple a lifestyle brand.

punchline.text: Two words saved a company. Think Different made Apple a religion.

quiz.question: What was Apple's financial state when 'Think Different' launched?

topics.title: De Beers: A Diamond Is Forever

hook.text: Before 1947, diamond engagement rings weren't universal.

buildup.text: Gerety worked at N.W. Ayer. She wrote the line late at night and almost discarded it. The agency nearly rejected it too.

discovery.text: The slogan linked diamonds to eternal love. Returning a diamond became unthinkable—forever means you keep it forever.

twist.text: Diamonds aren't rare. De Beers controlled supply. The slogan manufactured value for an abundant stone through pure copy.

climax.text: AdAge named it the #1 slogan of the 20th century. No other line of copy has generated more industry revenue.

punchline.text: Four words, invented a tradition, built a $72B industry.

quiz.question: Who wrote 'A Diamond Is Forever'?

hook.text: 'I'm Lovin' It' launched in 2003 with a Justin Timberlake jingle. It became McDonald's longest-running slogan ever.

buildup.text: A German agency—Heye & Partner—created the concept.

discovery.text: The 'ba da ba ba bah' jingle became a sonic logo worth billions. People sing it without realizing they're advertising.

twist.text: Critics called it grammatically lazy and unoriginal. But brand recall hit 90%. Academics lost; consumers voted.

climax.text: 20 years later, it's still the tagline. McDonald's has tried to replace it and can't.

punchline.text: Ba da ba ba bah. Four notes worth more than most brands.

quiz.question: In how many countries did 'I'm Lovin' It' launch?

hook.text: In 1973, a 23-year-old copywriter wrote 'Because I'm Worth It.' L'Oréal changed 'I'm' to 'You're.' A movement was born.

buildup.text: Ilon Specht wrote it as a response to women being told they didn't deserve premium products. It was a feminist act.

discovery.text: The slogan gives women permission to spend on themselves. It reframes a purchase as self-care, not vanity.

twist.text: In 2009, it evolved to 'Because We're Worth It'—adding community. Each pronoun shift reflected cultural change.

climax.text: The slogan has run for 50+ years across dozens of languages. Universal self-worth transcends culture.

punchline.text: A 23-year-old wrote a feminist slogan. It ran for 50 years.

quiz.question: What was the original pronoun in L'Oréal's slogan?

hook.text: 'I Like Ike' won Eisenhower the 1952 presidency. Three syllables, perfect rhythm, impossible to forget.

buildup.text: The slogan was paired with the first political TV jingle—an animated cartoon.

discovery.text: The rhyme made it chantable. Crowds at rallies sang it. The slogan spread orally, becoming a cultural phenomenon.

twist.text: Adlai Stevenson, his opponent, refused low-brow advertising. He lost badly.

climax.text: 'I Like Ike' proved that political branding follows the same rules as product branding: simplicity, emotion, rhythm.

punchline.text: Three syllables won a presidency. Political slogans are advertising.

quiz.question: What made 'I Like Ike' historically significant?
options: First political TV jingle and slogan campaign

hook.text: Obama's 2008 'Yes We Can' wasn't just a slogan—it was a promise. Three words made voters into participants.

buildup.text: Borrowed from farmworker leader Dolores Huerta's 'Sí, se puede,' the phrase had deep roots in American activism.

discovery.text: The slogan used the word 'we' to create collective identity. Voters felt ownership: this isn't his campaign—it's ours.

twist.text: A celebrity music video turned the speech into a viral hit. It reached 26 million views when viral meant something.

climax.text: The slogan transcended politics.

punchline.text: 'We' made it everyone's slogan. Collective identity won an election.

quiz.question: Where did 'Yes We Can' originate?
options: Dolores Huerta's 'Sí, se puede' farmworker movement

hook.text: Reagan used 'Let's Make America Great Again' in 1980. Trump shortened it to four words and a red hat in 2015.

buildup.text: MAGA is a nostalgia slogan. 'Again' implies a golden past that was lost. It triggers both longing and anger.

discovery.text: The slogan was trademarked days after the 2012 election—years before the campaign launched.

twist.text: The red hat became the logo. Supporters wore the slogan. It was the first slogan-as-fashion since Che Guevara T-shirts.

climax.text: Love it or hate it, MAGA proved that slogans can create tribal identity. The words became a movement, not just a phrase.

punchline.text: Four words on a hat created a political tribe. Slogans move nations.

quiz.question: Who first used a version of 'Make America Great Again'?

topics.title: Black Lives Matter as a Slogan

hook.text: Three words posted on Facebook in 2013 became the defining social movement slogan of the decade. Hashtag as manifesto.

buildup.text: Alicia Garza, Patrisse Cullors, and Opal Tometi created #BlackLivesMatter after Trayvon Martin's case. Digital born.

discovery.text: The slogan's power is its simplicity. It states a fact as a challenge. Disagreeing with it requires denying humanity.

twist.text: Counter-slogans like 'All Lives Matter' proved the original's potency. When a slogan forces a response, it dominates.

climax.text: By 2020, BLM appeared on murals, merch, and streets painted by mayors. The slogan became physical infrastructure.

punchline.text: Three words on Facebook became a global movement. That's slogan power.

quiz.question: Where was #BlackLivesMatter first posted?

hook.text: Printed in 1939, never used, discovered in 2000, then became the most reproduced poster of the 21st century.

buildup.text: The British government made it for wartime morale. Two and a half million copies were printed.

discovery.text: A bookseller found a copy in 2000 and printed it in her shop. Visitors wanted copies.

twist.text: The slogan became a meme template: 'Keep Calm and Code On,' 'Keep Calm and Eat Cake.' Parody made it immortal.

climax.text: It proved that a great slogan exists outside time. Sixty years in a box couldn't kill five words of perfect tone.

punchline.text: Lost for 60 years. Found. Went viral. Great copy is timeless.

quiz.question: When was 'Keep Calm and Carry On' originally printed?

hook.text: 'Just Do It.' 'Think Different.' 'Eat Fresh.' 'Obey Your Thirst.' The most powerful slogans are commands.

buildup.text: Imperative slogans give the reader a role. You're not a spectator—you're an actor. The verb creates action in the mind.

discovery.text: Research shows imperative sentences are processed faster than declaratives.

twist.text: Imperatives only work when the brand has earned the authority to command. A startup can't say 'Do It' like Nike can.

climax.text: The best imperatives feel like encouragement, not orders. 'Think Different' invites; 'Buy Now' demands. Tone matters.

punchline.text: Commands drive action. But only earned authority can command.

quiz.question: Why do imperative slogans work well?
options: They give the reader a role and are processed faster

hook.text: 'Think Different' is grammatically wrong. Is 'different' an adverb or adjective? The ambiguity makes you linger on it.

buildup.text: Ambiguous slogans invite interpretation.

discovery.text: 'Impossible Is Nothing' by Adidas works because the syntax is odd. You pause, reread, and think.

twist.text: Too much ambiguity confuses. 'The Quicker Picker Upper' (Bounty) is clear despite being playful.

climax.text: The best ambiguous slogans reward deeper thinking. 'Got Milk?' can mean 'Do you have milk?' or 'Have you got milk yet?'

punchline.text: Ambiguity makes you pause. That pause is where the brand lives.

quiz.question: Why can ambiguity in a slogan be effective?
options: It invites personal interpretation and creates a pause

hook.text: 'Don't Be Evil' was Google's motto. 'Impossible Is Nothing' denies limitation.

buildup.text: Negative slogans stand out because most advertising is relentlessly positive. The contrast makes them memorable.

discovery.text: Avis's 'We Try Harder' implied Hertz didn't try. The negative comparison was embedded in the positive claim.

twist.text: Google dropped 'Don't Be Evil' as its official motto in 2015. The slogan became a weapon critics used against them.

climax.text: Negative slogans are double-edged. They're memorable but provide ammunition. 'Don't be evil' invites 'But you are.'

punchline.text: Negatives grab attention. But they give critics a weapon too.

quiz.question: Why did Google drop 'Don't Be Evil'?
options: Critics used it as ammunition against the company
It was trademarked by someone else

hook.text: 'Got Milk?' 'Where's the Beef?' 'What's in Your Wallet?' Questions demand mental engagement.

buildup.text: Psychologists call it the 'instinctive elaboration' response.

discovery.text: Question slogans are interactive. The reader co-creates meaning by answering internally.

twist.text: Questions risk a wrong answer. 'Is Pepsi OK?' Diners answering 'No' reinforced a negative brand association for years.

climax.text: The best question slogans have only one answer—the brand.

punchline.text: Ask a question, own the answer. Questions engage the brain instantly.

quiz.question: Why do question slogans work so well?
options: The brain automatically seeks to answer questions

hook.text: KFC's 'Finger Lickin' Good' translated to 'Eat Your Fingers Off' in Chinese. Global slogans need local adaptation.

buildup.text: Pepsi's 'Come Alive' became 'Pepsi brings your ancestors back from the dead' in China.

discovery.text: Smart brands 'transcreate' rather than translate. They keep the feeling while changing the words completely.

twist.text: Some slogans need no translation. Nike's swoosh and 'Just Do It' work globally because the emotion is universal.

climax.text: Coca-Cola adapts its slogan per market.

punchline.text: Don't translate slogans. Transcreate them. Feeling, not words.

quiz.question: What is 'transcreation'?
options: Adapting the feeling of a message for another culture
Creating a new slogan for each country

topics.title: New Coke: The Taste of a New Generation Gone Wrong

hook.text: In 1985, Coca-Cola changed its formula and launched 'The Best Just Got Better.' 400,000 angry letters proved otherwise.

buildup.text: Pepsi's 'The Choice of a New Generation' had been winning blind taste tests. Coke panicked and reformulated.

discovery.text: The new slogan ignored what Coke actually was: nostalgia, tradition, Americana. No slogan could sell a betrayal.

twist.text: Coke brought back the original as 'Coca-Cola Classic' and sales soared.

climax.text: The lesson: a slogan can't fix a bad product decision. Copy serves the brand, not the other way around.

punchline.text: 400,000 angry letters. No slogan can sell a betrayal.

quiz.question: How many complaint letters did Coca-Cola receive about New Coke?

hook.text: 'Come Alive with the Pepsi Generation' sounded great in English.

buildup.text: The 1960s slogan aimed at youth energy. It worked in Western markets. International rollout was not tested locally.

discovery.text: The mistranslation story—possibly apocryphal—became a legendary cautionary tale taught in every advertising course.

twist.text: Even if the exact translation is debated, the principle is real: dozens of brands have suffered genuine translation.

climax.text: The lesson became standard practice: test slogans in every target market with native speakers before global launch.

punchline.text: Test locally or die globally. Translation disasters are preventable.

quiz.question: What lesson did Pepsi's translation issue teach?
options: Always test slogans with native speakers in target markets

hook.text: In 2014, Gap launched 'Dress Normal.' Customers wondered: are you calling us boring? The slogan insulted its audience.

buildup.text: Gap tried to celebrate everyday style. But 'normal' carries negative connotations—ordinary, unremarkable, bland.

discovery.text: Social media mocked it immediately. 'Dress Normal' became a punchline. The slogan was pulled within months.

twist.text: The concept wasn't wrong—Normcore was trending.

climax.text: Word choice killed a good strategy. 'Dress You' or 'Simply You' might have worked. 'Normal' was the wrong word.

punchline.text: One wrong word killed a campaign. 'Normal' isn't aspirational.

quiz.question: Why did Gap's 'Dress Normal' campaign fail?
options: 'Normal' has negative connotations that conflict with fashion's promise

hook.text: In 1985, Burger King spent $40 million on 'Where's Herb?'—a man who'd never eaten a Whopper. Nobody cared who Herb was.

buildup.text: The campaign asked customers to spot Herb in restaurants for prizes. It was a mystery game tied to the brand.

discovery.text: The problem: the concept emphasized NOT eating at Burger King. Herb's inexperience was the joke.

twist.text: When Herb was finally revealed on live TV, it was anticlimactic. $40 million for a man in glasses nobody remembered.

climax.text: AdAge called it 'the most elaborate advertising flop' of the 1980s. The slogan died, and so did the CMO's career.

punchline.text: $40 million wasted. Never make your brand the punchline.

quiz.question: Why did Burger King's 'Where's Herb?' campaign fail?
options: The concept emphasized not eating at Burger King

hook.text: Every failed slogan teaches the same lesson: the slogan must serve the brand. Not the creative team's ego.

buildup.text: Failed slogans share patterns: they insult the audience, they're too clever, they contradict the brand promise, or they.

discovery.text: The cure is testing. Every slogan should be tested with real customers before launch.

twist.text: But testing kills boldness. 'Think Different' would have tested poorly—it's grammatically wrong.

climax.text: The best approach: test to catch obvious failures, then trust creative instinct for the final call.

punchline.text: Test to avoid disasters. Trust instinct for greatness. Both matter.

quiz.question: What is the right balance for slogan development?
options: Test to avoid failures, trust instinct for the final call

topics.title: Dollar Shave Club: Our Blades Are Great

hook.text: A cheeky YouTube video in 2012 declared 'Our Blades Are F***ing Great.' Humor, honesty, and $1 razors built a $1B brand.

buildup.text: Michael Dubin shot the launch video for $4,500. It got 12,000 orders in 48 hours.

discovery.text: The slogan worked because it said what everyone was thinking: razor blades are overpriced—and ours are genuinely great.

twist.text: Gillette, the $10B incumbent, initially ignored them. By the time Gillette responded, DSC had 15% of the US market.

climax.text: Unilever bought Dollar Shave Club for $1 billion in 2016. A slogan and a video disrupted a century-old industry.

punchline.text: $4,500 video, $1B exit. Great copy beats great budgets.

quiz.question: How much did it cost to produce Dollar Shave Club's launch video?

hook.text: 'Belong Anywhere' reframed Airbnb from 'cheap hotel alternative' to 'global belonging.' The slogan elevated the brand.

buildup.text: Launched in 2014, the rebrand included a new logo (the Bélo) and a mission statement compressed into two words.

discovery.text: The word 'belong' is powerful. It taps into a fundamental human need—Maslow's third level.

twist.text: Critics said it was too abstract for a booking platform. But abstract slogans age better—they grow WITH the brand.

climax.text: As Airbnb expanded from rooms to experiences, 'Belong Anywhere' still worked.

punchline.text: Belong Anywhere. Two words bigger than any booking platform.

quiz.question: What human need does 'Belong Anywhere' tap into?

hook.text: 'Where Work Happens' positioned Slack as THE place for work—not one tool among many.

buildup.text: Slack launched in 2013 as a chat tool. The slogan elevated it to a platform—a destination, not just an app.

discovery.text: It's a declarative statement that feels like a fact. 'Where work happens' doesn't argue—it asserts.

twist.text: Slack later dropped it for 'Made for People.' The original was more powerful.

climax.text: The lesson: great slogans feel inevitable. 'Where Work Happens' sounded like it had always been true.

punchline.text: Declare a fact. Own a category. Confidence sells position.

quiz.question: What made 'Where Work Happens' effective?
options: It positioned Slack as THE place for work, not one tool among many

topics.title: Patagonia: We're in Business to Save Our Planet

hook.text: Patagonia's mission statement is its slogan. 'We're in Business to Save Our Home Planet.' Purpose as brand copy.

buildup.text: In an era where consumers distrust advertising, mission-driven slogans signal authenticity that traditional taglines.

discovery.text: Patagonia donates 1% of sales to environmental causes.

twist.text: Yvon Chouinard gave away the company to a climate trust. The founder's actions made the slogan undeniably authentic.

climax.text: Purpose slogans only work when proven. Greenwashing—fake purpose—destroys trust faster than no slogan at all.

punchline.text: Purpose as slogan. But only if the brand actually lives it.

quiz.question: What makes Patagonia's purpose-slogan credible?
options: Actions back it up: 1% donation, company given to climate trust

hook.text: In a world of TikTok, memes, and AI-generated content, do slogans still matter? The answer is yes—more than ever.

buildup.text: Attention spans are shrinking. The slogan—a compressed burst of brand meaning—is perfectly adapted to a distracted era.

discovery.text: Modern slogans live as hashtags, bios, and profile descriptions.

twist.text: AI can generate thousands of slogans instantly.

climax.text: The slogan is the smallest unit of brand strategy.

punchline.text: Shorter attention, bigger need. Slogans matter more, not less.

quiz.question: Why are slogans more important in the age of short attention?
options: They're the smallest unit of brand meaning, perfect for distracted audiences
